difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a clear necessary/sufficient confusion (treating a sufficient condition as necessary). Two answer choices are designed to share surface plausibility by involving conditionals; the student must track which one reverses the same conditional direction.
stimulus: Dr. Reyes noted that every patient who receives the new antiviral drug Velozine recovers from the infection within three days. Marcus recovered from his infection within three days. Therefore, Marcus must have received Velozine.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every employee who passes the certification exam is eligible for promotion. Daniela is eligible for promotion. Therefore, Daniela must have passed the certification exam.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every employee who passes the certification exam is eligible for promotion. Tomás passed the certification exam. Therefore, Tomás is eligible for promotion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No employee who fails the certification exam is eligible for promotion. Yuki failed the exam. Therefore, Yuki is not eligible for promotion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some employees who are eligible for promotion have not yet passed the certification exam. Renata is eligible for promotion. Therefore, Renata has probably not passed the certification exam.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most employees who pass the certification exam receive a salary increase within a year. Jerome received a salary increase within a year. Therefore, Jerome probably passed the certification exam.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats a sufficient condition (receiving Velozine → recovery) as if it were also necessary (recovery → received Velozine). This is affirming the consequent: if P then Q; Q; therefore P. Choice A commits the identical flaw — passing the exam is sufficient for eligibility, but the argument concludes from eligibility alone that the exam was passed.
explanations.A: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus exactly: the sufficient condition (passing exam → eligible) is treated as necessary (eligible → must have passed). This is affirming the consequent.
explanations.B: This is a valid modus ponens inference: if P then Q; P; therefore Q. No flaw.
explanations.C: This is a valid modus ponens with a negative conditional: no P→Q; Yuki is P; therefore Yuki is not Q. No flaw.
explanations.D: This introduces the quantifier 'some' and draws a probabilistic conclusion in the wrong direction, which resembles a base-rate reversal rather than a necessary/sufficient confusion. Different flaw.
explanations.E: This involves 'most' rather than 'every,' making it a base-rate reversal (Carpaccio-type flaw) rather than affirming the consequent. The stimulus uses a universal conditional, not a probabilistic claim.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole (compositional) fallacy — inferring that a property of each part must belong to the whole. Two answer choices involve similar subject matter and quantifier language, requiring the student to distinguish the compositional fallacy from a valid generalization and from a different quantifier error.
stimulus: Each individual chapter of Professor Aldana's new economics textbook is concise and easy to read. Therefore, the textbook as a whole must be concise and easy to read.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each tile in the mosaic is small and lightweight. Therefore, the mosaic as a whole is small and lightweight.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each tile in the mosaic was crafted by a skilled artisan. Therefore, the mosaic as a whole was crafted by skilled artisans.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mosaic contains hundreds of tiles. Most of the tiles are blue. Therefore, the mosaic is predominantly blue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each ingredient in the dish is healthful when eaten alone. However, some combinations of healthful ingredients can produce harmful chemical reactions. Therefore, this dish may not be healthful.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every individual musician in the orchestra performed flawlessly. Therefore, the audience gave the orchestra a standing ovation.

explanations.correct: The stimulus assumes that a property true of each part (concise, easy to read) must be true of the whole — the classic compositional fallacy. Choice A replicates this exactly: each tile is small and lightweight, but the whole mosaic need not be small or lightweight. The predicate 'small' is paradigmatically non-compositional.
explanations.A: Correct. Attributes 'small' and 'lightweight' to each tile and then illegitimately attributes the same properties to the whole mosaic — same compositional fallacy as the stimulus.
explanations.B: This is actually a valid inference for 'crafted by skilled artisans' — if each part was crafted by skilled artisans, the whole was crafted by skilled artisans. This is a distributive property that does transfer to the whole. No flaw.
explanations.C: This is a valid probabilistic inference from a majority of parts. No compositional fallacy — the conclusion ('predominantly blue') is appropriately hedged and follows from 'most tiles are blue.'
explanations.D: This explicitly acknowledges the non-compositional nature of the whole, making it an argument against the compositional fallacy. It does not commit the error; it warns against it.
explanations.E: This is a different flaw — it conflates the quality of individual performances with the audience's reaction, which involves an unwarranted causal leap rather than a part-to-whole attribution of properties.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a correlation-to-causation flaw in a policy context. Answer choices include one that reverses the causal direction (a related but distinct flaw) and one that is a valid inference, requiring students to identify the specific causal overreach rather than merely any causal misstep.
stimulus: Ever since the city of Hartwell introduced its community policing program two years ago, rates of reported property crime have dropped significantly. Clearly, the community policing program is responsible for the reduction in property crime.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Since the Morrow Valley school district began requiring students to wear uniforms three years ago, student test scores have risen steadily. The uniform policy must be the reason test scores have improved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Economists have found that cities with higher average incomes tend to have lower crime rates. Therefore, high incomes must prevent residents from committing crimes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The number of specialty coffee shops in Hartwell has grown in every year that the community policing program has been in place. Therefore, the coffee shops are causing crime rates to fall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hartwell's property crime rate is now lower than it was two years ago. The police chief was appointed two years ago. Therefore, the police chief must have been appointed because crime rates were falling.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hartwell's community policing program has been in place for two years and remains well-funded. Programs that remain well-funded for two or more years are generally considered successful. Therefore, the program is probably considered successful.

explanations.correct: The stimulus observes a temporal correlation (program introduced, then crime fell) and concludes the program caused the drop, ignoring alternative explanations. Choice A replicates this exactly: a policy was introduced, a positive outcome followed, and the policy is credited as the cause — the same post hoc, correlation-to-causation flaw.
explanations.A: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus: a new policy (uniforms) preceded an improvement (test scores), and the policy is concluded to be the cause — identical correlation-to-causation overreach with no consideration of confounding factors.
explanations.B: This commits a different causal flaw — it interprets a cross-sectional correlation (high income and low crime co-occur) as evidence that one prevents the other. Unlike the stimulus, which uses temporal sequence, this conflates correlation with causation in a non-temporal, cross-sectional way. Also, 'prevent' introduces a stronger causal claim than the stimulus's structure warrants.
explanations.C: This is a different flaw — it attributes causation to a factor (coffee shops) that is clearly a parallel trend, not even the policy being evaluated. The implausibility of the causal agent distinguishes this from the stimulus, which at least involves a plausible candidate.
explanations.D: This reverses the causal direction: it concludes the appointment was caused by the crime trend, whereas the stimulus concludes the policy caused the crime trend. This is reverse causation, a distinct flaw.
explanations.E: This is a valid deductive inference: the program meets the stated criteria for being considered successful. No causal claim and no flaw.
